title: Opening and Closing
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of embracing imperfection and uncertainty in Zen practice, encouraging listeners to let go of judgment and perfectionism by resting in the present moment. By cultivating a sense of wonderment and openness through inquiry and exploration, we can develop vulnerability and connection with ourselves and others, ultimately leading to deeper spiritual growth and understanding. This approach is illustrated through classic Zen myths, such as the story of Nanyu, which highlights the value of questioning and investigation in uncovering the truth.

sentences.text: Nice to see everyone.
Oh, how nice you could come back, Marilyn.
Welcome back.
How could I not come back?
You never left.

I'm really feeling full of appreciation and gratitude for the miracle that we could do this together, which is really enjoyable to me because my particular ball of conditioning trends much more strongly towards judgment and perfectionism.
So it's fun, it's really pleasant, when appreciation and acceptance are around.
I really appreciated Norman's remarks this morning about the miracle of just resting in these six senses.

In a more usual English construction it might be just contentment with life or just resting in life, but I think they very deliberately spoke about the six senses, because this idea of life is sort of an overlay on top of that, an idea that we have about who we are or what all this is.
But what if it was just resting in what we see, what we hear, what we smell, what we taste, what we touch, and what thoughts arise?
What if that was just enough?
That would be great.
Once in a while we can appreciate that.
And it's a great description of our intention and effort in Zazen too, isn't it?
In Zazen, what else is there to do but rest in the six senses?
If you try to do anything else, you're not too happy in Zazen.
Have you noticed that?
If you wish for some other data in your six senses, you may not get it.

I also wanted to bring up a Zen story that Dogen appreciated, but before I do I thought I would add a few postscripts to Norman's appreciation of a few of the people he mentioned who have passed away, and he also mentioned someone who has passed away from here.
I was thinking just before the talk that maybe a sangha is not really fully alive until its members start to die.
There's some sense of maturity, and some sense of finally being able to appreciate what we have once we lose it, once it starts to go.
I didn't know Jerome Peterson very well, but he was tremendously helpful to me in my famous first sesshin at San Francisco Zen Center.
It was famous because I was such a young and enthusiastic student that I caused tremendous internal mayhem the way I went about it, because I was just trying so hard.
I used to like to tell stories about it.
I think I spared you for a while the stories of my famous first sesshin, seven-day sesshin, so it's been long enough that I can trot out the old stories.
Maybe that's the actual work of giving a talk: you get to trot out your old stories in rotation.

So anyway, when I first got there I immediately looked at the schedule, which was more sitting than I had ever done, and I calculated very quickly in my mind how many sesshin periods there would be in the whole week, which is pretty easy: this many per day, and one in the beginning and the end.
Then I started a countdown with the first sesshin period, and I thought, okay, 77 to go.
That turns out to be not too terrible a thing to do if you happen to have had a pleasant experience.
Okay, 76 to go.
But if you have a really unpleasant experience in sesshin, it's a big problem, because then it's like, 68 more.
The other thing I discovered was, you did this as a kid, if you press your eyeballs for a while, you get these floaty visions and you can see things?
Well, it turns out if you get stressed out enough while you're sitting and get tense enough, you can create that phenomenon internally.
You're clenching on your eyeball with the muscles or something like that.
So I started having these visions, which weren't really visions, they were just tension.
Right across from me, in the opposite row, was Jerome, and I didn't really learn this lesson at the time.
Years later it seems like you appreciate the lessons that people offer you.

He would shamble in, I didn't really know him, I knew his name I think, and climb up, it was all on these raised platforms, he'd climb up on the tongue like that and settle down in this very odd kind of posture, and he would instantly go to sleep, too, that was the other part.
Maybe that was projecting, but it seemed like he was instantly sleeping.
He was so relaxed, it's true.
And here I was: I'm going to do this right, I'm going to do this right, I'm going to do this right, and seeing these things and so tense, and here's this senior member of the community just snoozing.
You'd think I would have noticed, you'd think I would have learned something at the time.
Each of us has to go through our own personal arc and learn from our own suffering, but later I really appreciated that teaching from Jerome of just snoozing through the whole sesshin.
Every period, some periods, I remember him for that.
And Blanche Hartman I knew a little better because I lived with them for a while at Green Gulch, and what I was remembering about Lou was his tremendous love for work.
I worked in the kitchen, and he used to come and give us little efficiency tips.
Very minute things, like when you reach for the measuring cup, if you hold your hand this way, it's better.

Or once he came and told us several times to be really attentive when you're at the counter and you have to turn around, or when you're at one table or one counter and you have to turn around to another table: think about which way you should turn, which way really feels right to turn.
At the time it seemed a little bothersome.
He was this guy.
I think most of the cooks were fairly young, as I was, and we thought we knew what we were doing, as you do when you're 22.
But later I appreciated, not the tips exactly, but the care, the love for the details and the feeling of work.
I know that he was a communist and a labor person and worked in many different trades.
He carried, I think, that love of work.
So I just want to add those two comments.
I didn't know Darlene or Wendy.
But then also, a little over a year ago we lost a member of our community, a man named Mark Livingston.
He was a very quiet, humble, big guy.
He was a laborer, so Lou made me think of him.
He was actually a union laborer.
That was his life's work, to be on the union call and then dig ditches and build walls and work with his hands.
He was very fast.
His friends called him Digger because he could dig a ditch faster than anybody you ever met, apparently.
And you never see him dig a ditch.
But here at the Dharma Hall, he built things.
The city required that we have, you've probably even noticed it, a concrete ramp.
There was a little three-inch step in the front that would have prevented a wheelchair, I guess, from coming in.
So we required this ramp, and none of us really knew how to make a concrete ramp.
I called the concrete guy, and he wanted thousands of dollars, and I wondered what to do.
Somehow Mark overheard a conversation.
He said, "I don't think I could do that."
He very quietly did, very humbly.
He did a lot of things like that, and he was also young.
He was in his late 50s when he died.
Several illnesses came together in his health history, and he died very quickly from an infection at the hospital.
What's sad about his death is that he has grown daughters in their mid-20s, but he also had a child by a second marriage who's now, I think, about 11, a little boy named Dixon.
I so appreciate Mark for his quiet work and dedication to practice.
I didn't find out until actually the funeral the many ways that he practiced over his life.
He didn't really talk about his understanding.
He just showed up, just sat, just worked.
The other thing I want to mention about Mark was we did a funeral for him, which was this huge affair at the labor hall.
It was a room that should have sat about 30, and there were about 100 people in there.
And all the body heat, it was so hot, but so loving, so warm at every level.
That was wonderful.
But that was for the friends and the family, who I think were still in shock.
They hadn't really felt yet that he was gone.
Then a couple of months ago we did a one-year memorial for him, and it was just the family and a few friends, and it was here, not at the labor hall.

One of his daughters, they have connections in Alaska, was in Alaska and couldn't make it down, so we set her up on a Skype video chat on a little laptop in the corner here, and she watched the whole thing.
She was able to see it and hear it.
For some reason she could hear us, but we couldn't hear her when she talked, so she was this little mute person inside the little screen.
Some of the younger family members carried her around for the rest of the event, down to the reception, and they had Amber in the little thing.
She's sitting on her couch just waving.
Several people in the family told me later that it really helped them a lot, that we could have that memorial service together.
So it makes you wonder, what can we offer, this strange Zen practice?
Someone was telling me earlier today that she was just really struck anew by how bizarre this is.
Strange robes and customs, and eat your food this way and not that way.
And yet somehow out of this bizarre situation, there's something that we can offer, something that really helps, really helps, and really helps in a situation where nothing else can help.
It's not very practical otherwise, and it's a little hard to explain or understand, as these strange Zen stories that Norman was bringing up remind us.
Last week I had the pleasure of visiting the Student Meditation Club at the University up the hill here, which meets every week at 4 o'clock on Friday.
They have one hour of meditation.
I guess this wasn't their usual room, so the attendance was a little bit low, at about 30, 35 college students.
They told me that usually they get 50 to 60 college students every week, sometimes more.
I'm not sure if the meditation they do every week would exactly feel the same as what we're doing here.
They have lots of different kinds of guided meditation, and visiting teachers from all traditions, which is a very open-hearted thing.
The two young men who organize it just somehow have a good sweet feeling.
I think people respond to their leadership in a nice way.
But I was struck by the amount of interest.
Of course it made me think about why they are so interested in meditation on the campus.
I think all of us who have any connection to young people know, at least anecdotally, that suffering and stress and depression on campus are really up, really way up.
I'm sure we could probably find some research on this, Toy probably knows, it probably has been studied.
It's probably scientifically valid that things are more stressful on the campus.
A few weeks ago there was a suicide on campus also, and last year or so I remember there was another suicide.
It could be that suicide on college campuses is becoming a fairly normal part of the situation.
I don't really know what the causes of all this are, but it's probably safe to assume that the increased levels of uncertainty in the world are a part of that.
The obvious uncertainty of the economy, if you're in a four-year degree program and your four-year degree is definitely not guaranteed to get you a job anymore.
The uncertainty of the changing climate.
And just maybe it's more and more clear, it's more clear to young people than it is to us, just how uncertain our survival is as a species.
It's really not certain.

It's a fairly intense situation, taking all these classes, needing to use their minds in a very particular way, very intensively, but I don't think they're taught anything about how to work with this uncertainty, how to respond to the uncertainty of this life.
So maybe that's what they're looking for at meditation club, I don't know, but it was quite encouraging to be there with them.
Of course the other part of this is that human beings, we do have this incredible ability to adapt, don't we?
To normalize to just about anything.
But it might be that there's a kind of tightening from a chronic stress that's taking its toll.
So anyway, one of the students made a little question and answer.
We did a little stretching and some zazen, and there's a question and answer time at the end.
One of the students asked me, "Well, what's the difference between Zen Buddhism and Theravada Buddhism?"
I didn't have a very good answer.

So I was thinking later, it's probably really unique to Zen Buddhism, or maybe to our particular lineage family, that you can practice very seriously for 20 to 25 years, and somebody will ask you, "Well, what's Zen Buddhism about?"
It's like there's no answer.
With anything else, wouldn't you have an answer?
You could categorize it or say, "Oh, it's such and so, it's just like this or it's that."
So I fumbled around and said some clichéd stuff: Theravada Buddhism emphasizing individual liberation and Mahayana Buddhism emphasizing compassion, and all this.
But I wasn't very satisfied with that.
Finally I had to resort to, "Well, they wear orange robes and we wear black robes," just so I could get on to another topic.
So I went to Master Dogen for advice, and I looked at his writings.
What is this tradition?
This tradition comes to us from Dogen.
How do we understand it?
How do we express it?
He quickly reminded me that part of why it's a little hard to answer a question like that is that our way of understanding seems to be a way of questions, much more than answers.
It's a way of working with phrases, a way of inquiry and a sort of spaciousness.
Zen teachings don't exactly say anything.
They have a quality of pointing to something beyond what you can hold in a narrow view.
For sure the bedrock of Buddha's teaching on suffering is there.
At least we assume it's there.

If you look carefully at Dogen, which I didn't know what that was before, I don't know if anywhere (we can ask later) in all of his vast writings he ever talked about the Four Noble Truths or Mindfulness or Insight.
I don't think so.
And he wrote a lot, so we have a pretty good sense of his whole corpus and his whole way of teaching through his career.
But it really is clear from the feeling that that is underneath all of this.
It's not presented as teachings to work with in a direct, sequential or stepwise way.
It's implied as something to make space for, vast room for the unfolding of our heart and our understanding, driven by our suffering, by the ways that things are not quite what.
And of course in Dogen Zen, the most obvious expression of this spaciousness is Zazen.
As you well know, he was a big fan of Zazen.
But that Zazen extends much more broadly than sitting on a cushion for 30 minutes until the bell.
It's a much more continuous, all-encompassing practice.
So sometimes in the sesshin we talk about seeing if you can extend your Zazen a little more, have a sense of continuity with your Zazen.
Then when the bell rings at the end of the period, it's not like me at 22: "Whew, check one more off.
Thank God."
And that thought may arise, that's okay.
That thought arising is included in this miracle of contentment with the six senses, right?
A thought like that could arise.
You have all kinds of thoughts.
But don't let it knock you off your seat.
Have a sense that Zazen is just changing position now.
Zazen is just transforming in some way.
Zazen is fluffing my cushion now.
Zazen is standing up.

So I dug around a little more in Dogen and found one of his many favorite stories, which he talks about over and over again in both his collection of essays, Shobogenzo, and also in a collection of his Dharma talks jotted down by his students.
Great big thick books.
Here's one of the stories he appreciated, which he spoke about and wrote about many times.
It involves a student formerly known as Nanyue, now henceforth known as something like Nanyu.
Nanyu, and it's rising on the last tone, it sounds like.
Not only do Chinese have these confusing tones that don't transliterate to English very well, it also matters what level the tone is and whether it goes up and down.
If you said Nanyu, it's one thing, and Nanyu is somebody else, so I'll try to say it right.
*Nanyu is the student of the famous Huineng, the sixth ancestor.
Nanyu visited the sixth ancestor, Huineng, and Huineng asked him, "Where do you come from?"
Nanyu said, "I come from the National Teacher An on Mount Song."
Huineng said, "What is it that thus comes?
What is it that thus comes?"
Master Nanyu was without means to answer.
After studying with Huineng for eight years, he finally understood the previous conversation.*
It's like me thinking about Jerome Patterson 20 years ago.
Finally you understand.
*Therefore he announced to the ancestor, Huineng, "I've understood what you put to me when I first came: 'What is it that thus comes?'" Huineng said, "How do you understand it?"
Nanyu replied, "To say it's like anything wouldn't hit it."
Huineng said, "Then is it contingent on practice and realization?"
Nanyu answered, "It is not without practice and realization, but it's not defiled by them."
Huineng said, "Just this not defiled is what the Buddhas bear in mind.
You're also like this.
I'm also like this.
All the ancestors of the Western Heavens are like this."*
The Western Heavens turn out to be India.
So the monk arrives at the monastery.
This is a very classic, mythic Zen story.
The monk arrives and gets an audience with the teacher.
The teacher starts with a standard question, "Where do you come from?" which has an obvious conventional meaning and a deeper meaning.
He says where he comes from: the National Teacher on Mount Song.
The teacher hears this and then asks another question.
So it's questions, it's questions.
What is it?
What is it that thus comes?
What is this?
It's a little hard to translate this phrase exactly.
"Thus comes" sounds a little funny to us in English.
And the student says, "Oh, I don't know."
So he stays to practice for eight years.
Of course these are myths, and it's very compressed.
A lot more happened in those eight years than these lines tell us.
It seems unlikely, really, that one went on one's first encounter ever with a teacher and received just the perfect practice question, a question that really catches your attention in a deep way.
So you don't just set it down, forget about it, or get busy and go on to other things.
Defend yourself.
Figure the teacher doesn't know what he's talking about.
And so on.
Instead the question just gets a hold of your heart.
You're also lucky in the story here to have a good situation for practice.
Maybe we're also lucky in that same way, where there's a lot of support.
Where you can feel in the air, "This is a place where I could investigate this.
These are people I could investigate this with.
This is a teacher that I could receive support from in this question."
So it does seem unlikely, practically speaking, that it would be that straightforward.
But it's written that way, so let's enjoy that myth.
It's the myth of the perfect practice, the perfect teacher and the perfect student.
This mythic quality is very powerful to us, and it's something we treasure in our tradition.
But it's also a little bit problematic.
Just lately, in the American Zen world, several long-standing Zen scandals have really broken.
Scandals involving sexual activity between teachers and students, male teachers and students.
Teachers who I'm sure, in some way, were mythologized by themselves and by the sanghas, and by just the times that they came into practice in America.
It appears from our experience there that leaning too much into this myth really messes us up.
It really gets us confused.
We lose our common sense.
The precepts get tangled and lost.
And there's at least one suicide mixed into those scandals as well.
So the good news is that some scandals are seen in the light of day, and people seem to be a lot less willing to be polite and not say anything.
It's a little bit bound up in the internet, actually.
The internet seems to be in play in a positive way.
Isn't that nice?
The internet can be positive sometimes.
But you can't hide stuff like that anymore.
Things that used to be private letters sent in an envelope, on a piece of paper stuck in a file, are now on a blog.
So if you do something shaky in your conduct, everyone on the internet can read about it.
Anyway, I was just thinking that we need both, right?
We can benefit from really treasuring this mythic power of the just-rightness of Zen teaching, and being a little bit careful.
If you're in the dokusan room with Huineng or Nanyu, and they do something inappropriate, please do not assume that it's a great teaching.
Tell somebody.
Because it really seems like we do need a mythic life.
We're in some way wired up as mythic animals.
Our big brains can process so much sensory data and construct so many ideas and constructs at such incredible speed, and yet we really suffer when we're stuck in that way of life.
We need this sense of something bigger, something deeper that seems to arise in myth.
And so we're there.
We're in the room with Nanyu when he enters the teacher's room in our monastery in southern China in about 700 A.D.
We're right there.
We can see how Huineng sees a settled practitioner coming in front of him, and he asks the standard question, "Where are you from?"
So where are you from?
Is the whole story that you came from Bellingham or Vancouver or Seattle or Bainbridge Island or somewhere?
Is that where you're from?
What is the full feeling of that question in your heart when you hear that?
Where are you from?
Where do you come from?
In our exchange, they didn't stay on that first question.
Maybe it was in some way a stepping stone to the second question, this deep question that activated the practice of Nanyu for eight years.
And then I guess he stayed seven years more, for 15 years.
Huineng probably learned something from his answer about the National Teacher An and Mount Song.
Maybe the world of Chinese Zen in the eighth century wasn't so big, probably.
He probably learned something about what Nanyu's training would have been from how he said it, something about what his relationship was with the practice and with that place.
And so Huineng asks another question, "What is it that thus comes?"
I've also seen this translated as, "What is it that has come like this?"
I broke out my online Chinese dictionary and tried to figure it out myself, and I came up with something like, "Just this matter just comes."
But there are a couple of characters that meant rope that I couldn't figure out, so take that with a grain of salt.
There are compounds, and I don't know enough to really figure it out.
It's so interesting, too, to think about the layers of language that we're resting on doing this practice here in Bellingham, Washington in 2011.
It's coming down to us from old writings in an Asian language that were directed so differently from the romance languages.
It's one of the things that we appreciated a lot when we were in Japan last summer, just how all the layers of language and meaning.
But maybe we can just boil it down to a simpler question that really is very practical for us to practice with.
What is it?
What is it?
You can actually practice with that in Zazen if you want to.
Maybe on an exhalation: What is it?
Maybe just after a while, just a sense of wonderment, of the miracle.
Because "What is it?" is another way of saying the same teaching about the miracle.
Maybe in some ways working with such a question or such a phrase can be helpful to us when we get a little stuck on ourselves.
Because we think we know so much, don't we?
We think we know who we are, what we're doing, why we're here.
After we practice for a couple of years we think we know how practice is supposed to go and how sesshin is supposed to go.
You should see all the little suggestions we get when we run the big sesshins.
"You should do it this way, you should do it that way."
Because we all know so much.
Sweet, actually.
We've gotten to where it's sweet; before, it would piss us off.
It's sweet.
But what if we meet all this knowing with a question like that, where there isn't really an answer in that way?
What if we were to drop in to that sense?
What is it?
In every moment, feeling that through this agency of the six senses.
What is that feeling in the body?
What is that emotion?
What is that thought arising?
What is it without any of those categories?
Just a sense of inquiry.
Another Zen poem that gets chanted a lot says:
*The matter is not in the words, yet it responds to the inquiring impulse.
The matter is not in the words, yet it responds to the inquiring impulse.*
So I really didn't have any words for my college friend.
But I recognized her inquiring impulse in some way, and it brought up my inquiring impulse.
Together we had a moment of inquiry [unclear: "up to center the talk"].
Another recent event for me that is at play here is that a couple of weeks ago I was in Massachusetts.
I was in Worcester, Worcester, Massachusetts, near Boston, at a training on teaching mindfulness in the style of John Kabat-Zinn: Mindfulness Based Stress Reduction.
Two teachers were really great.
It was a wonderful training, very deep practice.
I want to name the two trainers because they were such good teachers and practitioners.
They were Melissa Blacker and Florence Malio Meyer.
It's really a great style of practice, a secular style of Buddhism.
I was very skeptical at first getting involved with these guys.
But they really have a deep sense of the way.
They have their own particular language that they use.
"Languaging," they call it.
They make up these funny terms.
It's kind of cute.
But anyway, as part of their languaging they ban themselves from ever mentioning any Dharma teachers.
But Dharma seems to need teachings, right?
So they use poetry instead.
So they elevate poetry as Dharma teaching, which works fine.
Their very favorite poet is Rumi, so they're always quoting Rumi.
I think I know something.
Do I know something?
This sense of opening and closing and zazen made me think of a poem they read us by Rumi called "Bird Wings."
He wrote in the 12th century, maybe?
I forget.
A Persian poet.
*Your grief for what you've lost lifts a mirror up to where you are bravely working, expecting the worst.
You look, here's a joyful face you've been wanting to see.
Your hand opens and closes and opens and closes.
If there were always a fist or always stretched open, you would be paralyzed.
Your deepest presence is in every small contracting and expanding, the two as beautifully balanced and coordinated as bird wings.*
*Your grief for what you've lost lifts a mirror up to where you are bravely working, expecting the worst.
You look and instead, here's the joyful face you've been wanting to see.
Your hand opens and closes and opens and closes.
If there were always a fist or always stretched open, your deepest presence is in every small contracting and expanding, the two as beautifully balanced and coordinated as bird wings.*
What a wonderful teaching for us.
I think maybe we come into this practice with a misunderstanding, a kind of "supposed to" point of view: that we're supposed to be opening.
Not opening enough?
What's wrong with you?
My roomies are reminding us that there's no flow possible here.
Being stuck open, or stuck closed, is still stuck.
Thich Nhat Hanh talks about there being a kind of psychic circulation.
Things need to be able to circulate, opening and closing.
Sometimes it is really appropriate and really good to close up, to protect ourselves.
Sometimes that is skillful: safety, the drawbridge has to come up.
We may need to withdraw, and we sometimes use the English word "retreat" for this activity we're doing this weekend.
Sesshin and retreat are very different words, but sometimes we say retreat, and in some ways we're hiding from our regular life.
We're retreating this weekend.
No phone calls, we hope.
I hope you can reduce your phone calls.
No internet, no work, a little less involvement with family, and all these things.
So we're in some ways closing to make space for opening.
That retreat and advance, withdraw and letting go, are included in the full range of human experience.
And that idea here, as Norman was suggesting this morning, is not to never be anything other than ourself.
One last point and we'll get back to our Zen story.
Someone sent me a reference to the work of a really wonderful psychologist recently named Brene Brown.
Have you heard of Brene Brown?
She's at the University of Texas, somewhere, Austin maybe.
Her research is on vulnerability.
She's a researcher into vulnerability.
She suggests, kind of like I was feeling on campus, that as a society we're becoming less and less tolerant of vulnerability.
We can't tolerate feeling vulnerable.
There's more closing than opening going on.
We don't feel safe enough to be vulnerable, and as a result we're more and more missing out on the possibility of our life.
What she calls vulnerability, she says, is misunderstood by us as a kind of weakness: to be vulnerable is to be weak.
But actually vulnerability is the birthplace of joy and love, belonging, creativity and faith.
She had some interesting points about why she thinks this is the case, and one of them was that they do psychological experiments and have people respond to things.
She says in their experiments they can clearly see an increase in people viewing joy as foreboding.
Joy as foreboding.
By this she means, if something good happens, you're worried something bad's about to happen.
Do you know what I mean?
Does this happen to us?
She says this has become much more prevalent, that we can't just feel joy.
It's joy with fear.
We're compelled in our inner life to catastrophize and complain, in order to beat vulnerability to the punch, is the way she put it in the talk.
If I can be unhappy before I get disappointed, then I won't be so disappointed.
Right?
It's a kind of lifestyle, and then complain.
It's sad, it's really sad to think about.
And then the other option is to use perfectionism as a kind of shield, so that maybe you could actually hide from vulnerability if you were perfect enough, or appeared to be perfect enough.
One of the most telling things in her research, or in the lecture, was that they looked at people in recovery from addiction and at what kinds of experiences tend to trigger people to use again.
What they found was that a very happy event is just as likely as an unhappy event to trigger relapse.
The conclusion she draws from that is that there's a numbing response to suffering, but that numbing is universal.
You can't just numb the dark emotions and still be open to happiness.
It's actually not possible, she thinks, for humans to repress the unhappy things and try to get happy things poured in.
She said if you're reducing your ability to tolerate and experience unhappiness, you're also reducing your ability to experience and tolerate happiness.
You actually can't tolerate happiness, and that's the result of not being able to be vulnerable.
So I thought that was really compelling.
It's also worth noting that in these exchanges, in these Zen stories, at first they seem a little stilted and cold.
The style's a little funny in the translation.
But as we penetrate these stories and think about our own experience in sangha life, we realize that what Brene Brown said about vulnerability being involved in faith is really true.
There's a lot of vulnerability in these stories.
This monk presents himself to the great teacher and is really willing to be vulnerable, to listen, to open to whatever is being taught.
When this odd question, "What is it that thus comes?", strikes Nanya, he's able to be open and vulnerable with that.
He can stay with that.
He doesn't bluster, he doesn't cover up, he doesn't stomp out and leave, although sometimes they do stomp out and leave.
But usually they're making another point in some other way.
He says, "Oh, thank you, teacher."
And the teacher was also vulnerable.
Norman's story this morning was very much that way, the teacher asking the student, "Please help me to understand."
And so Nanya stays to live and practice at Huineng's monastery for eight years, practicing with this question: what is it, what is it that thus comes?
Since this is written in shorthand, it sounds like he sat down on his zafu for eight years, and they just gave him food once a day.

What is it?

Gone.

verbatim.text: Nice to see everyone. Oh, how nice you could come back, Marilyn. Welcome back. How could I not come back? You never left. by the ways that things are not quite what. And of course in Dogen Zen, the sort of most obvious expression of this spaciousness is Zazen. So as you well know, he was a big fan of Zazen.
